blog.title: The Honest GPU Buying Guide for 2026
blog.excerpt: Which graphics card you should actually buy depends on your monitor, not your budget. Here is how to work backwards from the panel you already own.
blog.body: [{"type":"paragraph","text":"The most expensive mistake in PC building is buying a graphics card that your monitor cannot exploit. A card that renders 240 frames per second attached to a 60 Hz panel delivers exactly 60 of them to your eyes. You have paid for 180 frames that no one will ever see."},{"type":"heading","text":"Start with the panel, not the card"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Write down two numbers before you shop: your monitor’s native resolution and its maximum refresh rate. Those two numbers define the entire useful range of graphics cards for you. Everything above that range is waste, and everything below is compromise you will feel every day."},{"type":"list","items":["1080p at 144–240 Hz — an RTX 5060 Ti or RX 9060 XT saturates this comfortably in most titles.","1440p at 144–180 Hz — the RTX 5070 class is the value peak; this is where most buyers should land.","1440p at 240 Hz or 4K at 120 Hz — RTX 5080 class, and expect to use upscaling in demanding titles.","4K at 144 Hz with ray tracing — RTX 5090 class, and even then frame generation is doing real work."]},{"type":"heading","text":"VRAM is the specification that ages worst"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Compute performance degrades gracefully — an older card simply renders fewer frames. Insufficient VRAM degrades catastrophically: textures fail to load, frame times spike, and the game stutters in a way no settings adjustment fully fixes. For a card you intend to keep three years or more, 12 GB is the realistic floor at 1440p and 16 GB at 4K."},{"type":"quote","text":"We have replaced more cards for running out of memory than for running out of speed. Buy the VRAM you will need in year three, not the frame rate you want in month one."},{"type":"heading","text":"Check your power supply standard, not just its wattage"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Modern cards draw brief transient spikes far above their rated power — sometimes double, for microseconds. An older ATX 2.x supply may trip its protection circuit on those spikes even when its wattage rating looks generous on paper. The ATX 3.1 standard exists specifically to handle this behaviour. Before you buy a card, check which standard your supply implements. It matters more than the number on the box."},{"type":"image","src":"products/nvidia-rtx.webp","alt":"Modern triple-fan graphics card installed in a PC","caption":"Check length and slot clearance against your case before ordering — many current cards exceed 330 mm."},{"type":"heading","text":"What we would actually recommend"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For the majority of buyers walking into our showroom, an RTX 5070-class card attached to a good 1440p high-refresh monitor produces the most satisfying result per rupee spent. If your budget is tight, spend it on the monitor first and the card second — a great panel makes a mid-range card feel excellent, while a weak panel makes a flagship card feel pointless."}]

blog.title: DDR5 vs DDR4: What Actually Matters in 2026
blog.excerpt: Faster memory sells well on a spec sheet. Here is where it makes a measurable difference to your work, and where it genuinely does not.
blog.body: [{"type":"paragraph","text":"DDR5 has been the default for new builds for a while now, but the question we get asked most often is whether it is worth upgrading an existing DDR4 machine. The answer depends almost entirely on what you do with the computer."},{"type":"heading","text":"Where DDR5 makes a real difference"},{"type":"list","items":["CPUs with large integrated graphics — the iGPU shares system memory, so bandwidth directly becomes frame rate.","Video editing with high-bitrate footage, where timeline scrubbing is bandwidth-bound.","Compilation and simulation workloads that stream large datasets through the cache hierarchy.","Any workload where you need more than 64 GB — DDR5 module capacities simply go higher."]},{"type":"heading","text":"Where it barely registers"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In GPU-bound gaming at 1440p or 4K, the difference between a good DDR4 kit and a good DDR5 kit is typically within a few percent — often inside run-to-run variance. If you are playing at high resolution with a discrete card, memory generation is not your constraint and upgrading will not feel like anything."},{"type":"quote","text":"Capacity beats speed for almost everyone. 32 GB of moderately fast memory outperforms 16 GB of very fast memory the moment you open a second application."},{"type":"heading","text":"The timing trap"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A DDR5-8000 kit with loose timings can be slower in practice than a DDR5-6000 kit with tight ones, because true latency is a function of both frequency and cycles. Multiply the CAS latency by 2000 and divide by the data rate to get latency in nanoseconds — that number is what your CPU actually waits for. Compare kits that way and the marketing headline numbers stop being persuasive."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One practical note: whatever kit you buy, check it against your motherboard’s qualified vendor list, and buy it as a matched kit rather than two separate modules. Two single sticks bought separately are not guaranteed to run together at their rated profile, and diagnosing that instability afterwards is genuinely tedious."}]

blog.title: Why Your PC Is Loud — And the Five-Minute Fix
blog.excerpt: Most noisy computers are not badly cooled. They are badly configured. Here is the diagnostic sequence we use on every machine that comes in.
blog.body: [{"type":"paragraph","text":"A computer that sounds like a hairdryer is usually not short of cooling capacity. It is running a default fan curve that ramps aggressively on brief temperature spikes, chasing a number that does not matter."},{"type":"heading","text":"Step one: identify which fan is loud"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Open your case and briefly stop each fan with a finger — carefully, and only for a second. The one whose silence you notice is the culprit. It is usually the CPU cooler or the graphics card, rarely a case fan."},{"type":"heading","text":"Step two: flatten the curve"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most stock fan curves react to instantaneous temperature, which spikes constantly during normal use. The result is audible surging — far more annoying than steady noise. In your BIOS, set a fan step-up and step-down delay of two to four seconds and flatten the slope below 70 °C. Modern processors are designed to run at 80 °C indefinitely; there is no need to fight brief excursions."},{"type":"list","items":["Set a floor of around 30% duty cycle so fans never fully stop and restart audibly.","Hold that floor to 65–70 °C, then ramp linearly to 100% at 90 °C.","Apply a 3-second hysteresis so brief spikes do not trigger a ramp at all.","Set the case fans slightly higher than the CPU fan to maintain positive pressure and reduce dust."]},{"type":"heading","text":"Step three: check the paste, then the dust"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Thermal paste dries out over roughly three to four years. If your machine is older than that and temperatures climb quickly under load, a repaste often drops peak temperatures by 8–15 °C — which lets the whole fan curve sit lower. Dust filters come second: clean them monthly, and they will do more for noise than any component upgrade."}]

blog.title: Is PCIe Gen5 Storage Worth It Yet?
blog.excerpt: Gen5 drives post spectacular sequential numbers. Whether you will ever notice depends on one specific characteristic of your workload.
blog.body: [{"type":"paragraph","text":"A Gen5 NVMe drive will happily report 14,000 MB/s in a benchmark. That number is real, and for most people it is also irrelevant — because almost nothing you do all day consists of reading one enormous contiguous file."},{"type":"heading","text":"Sequential versus random, and why it matters"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Application launches, operating system behaviour and game loading are dominated by small random reads, not large sequential ones. Random read performance has improved far more modestly between generations than the headline sequential figures suggest. This is why a Gen5 drive often feels identical to a good Gen4 drive in daily use."},{"type":"heading","text":"Where Gen5 genuinely earns its price"},{"type":"list","items":["Video editing scratch disks handling multiple high-bitrate 8K streams simultaneously.","Loading large AI model weights into memory, where the file genuinely is one enormous sequential read.","Scientific datasets and database work with large sequential scan patterns.","Moving very large files between two Gen5 drives — a case where both ends can sustain the rate."]},{"type":"quote","text":"For gaming and general use, put the money into capacity instead. A 2 TB Gen4 drive will improve your life more than a 1 TB Gen5 drive."},{"type":"heading","text":"The thermal caveat nobody mentions"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Gen5 drives run hot enough that they will throttle without a heatsink and meaningful airflow — at which point they perform like a Gen4 drive while having cost considerably more. If your motherboard lacks an integrated M.2 heatsink over the relevant slot, budget for one, and make sure there is actual air movement across it."}]

blog.title: Building Your First PC: The Order That Prevents Mistakes
blog.excerpt: Assembly sequence matters more than most guides admit. This is the order we use on the bench, and why each step comes where it does.
blog.body: [{"type":"paragraph","text":"Almost every first-build problem we see traces back to assembly order rather than technique. Installing components in the wrong sequence forces you to work in cramped spaces, and cramped work is where cables get missed and standoffs get forgotten."},{"type":"heading","text":"Build outside the case first"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Mount the CPU, memory and the primary M.2 drive onto the motherboard while it is still on the box it came in. Everything is accessible, well-lit and easy to inspect. Then — and this is the step most guides skip — connect the power supply and a monitor and confirm it POSTs before it goes anywhere near the case."},{"type":"list","items":["CPU into the socket first — align the triangle marker, never force the retention arm.","Memory next, in slots 2 and 4 counting from the CPU, unless your manual says otherwise.","Primary M.2 drive into the top slot, which is almost always the one wired directly to the CPU.","Test POST on the bench. Finding a dead component now saves an hour of disassembly later.","CPU cooler after the POST test — mounting it first blocks access to everything around the socket."]},{"type":"heading","text":"Then the case, in this order"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Install the power supply first, then route every cable you will need before the motherboard goes in — the space behind the tray is far easier to work in while it is empty. Fit the motherboard next, then the graphics card last, because a modern card physically blocks access to the lower half of the board."},{"type":"quote","text":"If you find yourself pushing hard, stop. Nothing in a PC build requires force. Something is misaligned, and forcing it is how sockets get damaged."},{"type":"heading","text":"Before you close the panel"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Run through a short checklist: both CPU power connectors seated, all PCIe power cables fully clicked in, front panel headers matched to the manual, no fan cable in a fan blade, and no standoff sitting where the board has no mounting hole. That last one causes a short and is genuinely difficult to diagnose afterwards."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Once it boots, go straight into the BIOS and enable your memory profile — XMP on Intel, EXPO on AMD. Memory runs at a conservative default speed until you do, and a surprising number of otherwise well-built machines run for years without anyone ever turning it on."}]

blog.title: Specifying a Workstation for Local AI Models
blog.excerpt: VRAM capacity determines what you can run. Everything else determines how fast. Here is how to size a machine against actual model requirements.
blog.body: [{"type":"paragraph","text":"When clients ask us to specify a machine for running language models locally, the conversation almost always starts in the wrong place — with the processor. For inference and fine-tuning, VRAM capacity is the binary constraint: either the model fits, or it does not run at all."},{"type":"heading","text":"Sizing VRAM against model size"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"As a working approximation, a model quantised to 4-bit needs roughly half its parameter count in gigabytes of VRAM, plus headroom for context. A 70B-parameter model at 4-bit therefore wants around 40 GB before context, which is why 48 GB professional cards are the practical entry point for that class, and why two of them opens up considerably more."},{"type":"list","items":["7B–13B models — 12 to 16 GB is comfortable; a consumer card handles this well.","30B–34B models — 24 GB at 4-bit, with limited context headroom.","70B models — 48 GB minimum at 4-bit; 96 GB for usable context lengths.","Fine-tuning rather than inference — budget roughly double the inference requirement."]},{"type":"heading","text":"What matters after VRAM"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Memory bandwidth determines tokens per second once the model fits. System RAM should be at least equal to total VRAM, because model loading passes through it. Storage matters more than people expect: loading a 40 GB model from a slow drive is a genuinely noticeable wait, repeated every time you switch models."},{"type":"quote","text":"Two clients in the last year bought high-end processors and mid-range GPUs for AI work. Both had to replace the GPU within four months. The processor is rarely the constraint."},{"type":"heading","text":"The infrastructure question people forget"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A dual-GPU training workstation can draw well over 1.5 kW sustained. That has three practical consequences: it needs a dedicated electrical circuit, it will meaningfully heat the room it sits in, and it is loud under sustained load. We carry out an electrical and thermal survey before quoting these machines, because discovering the circuit cannot support it after delivery is an expensive way to learn."}]

blog.title: How to Procure Office PCs Without Regretting It in Year Three
blog.excerpt: The cheapest desktop is rarely the cheapest desktop. A framework for evaluating business machines on total cost rather than sticker price.
blog.body: [{"type":"paragraph","text":"Office hardware procurement is usually evaluated on unit price, because that is the number on the quote. Three years later the same organisation is paying for early replacements, support hours and productivity lost to slow machines — costs that never appeared on the original comparison."},{"type":"heading","text":"Specify for year three, not day one"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A machine with 8 GB of memory is adequate the day it is delivered and inadequate within eighteen months, as applications grow and staff keep more browser tabs open. Specifying 16 GB adds a modest amount per unit and typically extends useful service life by two years. That is the single highest-leverage decision in the whole specification."},{"type":"list","items":["Memory — 16 GB minimum, with free slots so an upgrade does not mean discarding modules.","Storage — NVMe rather than SATA; the difference in daily responsiveness is immediately obvious to users.","Warranty — onsite rather than carry-in. Staff time spent transporting machines is a real cost.","Standardisation — one identical configuration across the fleet makes imaging, support and spares far cheaper."]},{"type":"heading","text":"Insist on BOM consistency in writing"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many suppliers quote a specification, not a bill of materials — which permits them to substitute components between units as stock varies. The result is a fleet that is nominally identical but behaves differently machine to machine, which makes imaging unreliable and support unpredictable. Ask for the exact component list, and ask for it to be contractual."},{"type":"quote","text":"Ask any prospective supplier for the exact bill of materials, in writing, with a commitment that it will not change across the order. How they respond tells you most of what you need to know."},{"type":"heading","text":"Plan disposal before you buy"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Data-bearing devices leaving your premises carry real regulatory exposure. Agree the disposal process at procurement time — certified wiping to a recognised standard, with certificates issued per serial number. Retrofitting a compliant disposal process three years later, under audit pressure, is considerably more painful than specifying it upfront."}]

blog.title: RTX 50 Series: Real Availability and Pricing in India
blog.excerpt: What is actually on shelves in Trichy this month, what the street price looks like, and which models are worth waiting for.
blog.body: [{"type":"paragraph","text":"Launch MSRPs and Indian street prices have historically diverged for the first few months of any GPU generation. Here is what we are actually seeing across authorised distribution this month, rather than what the launch slides promised."},{"type":"heading","text":"Current stock position"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Mid-range cards are in genuine supply and trading close to expected pricing. The flagship tier remains allocation-limited, which means street prices sit above MSRP and availability is inconsistent week to week. If you are buying at the top of the stack, plan on reserving rather than walking in."},{"type":"list","items":["RTX 5060 Ti and RTX 5070 — readily available, pricing stable across board partners.","RTX 5070 Ti — available in limited quantity, with pricing varying meaningfully by partner.","RTX 5080 — allocation-limited; we recommend reserving rather than waiting for walk-in stock.","RTX 5090 — scarce, and priced accordingly. Consider whether an RTX 5080 genuinely constrains you first."]},{"type":"heading","text":"A note on grey imports"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Cards imported outside authorised distribution carry no local warranty, and in practice a failure means dealing with a foreign RMA process at your own cost. The saving is typically 8–12%; the exposure is the full replacement cost. We do not stock them, and we would advise against them at current price differentials."}]

faqs.question: Do you publish prices?
faqs.answer: Not on the website. Component prices move week to week and we serve both trade and retail customers at different rates, so a published figure would be out of date or wrong for you. Call or WhatsApp +91 97914 30774 with what you need and you will get a current price the same day.

faqs.question: Do you sell wholesale as well as retail?
faqs.answer: Yes. We supply service shops, resellers and integrators at trade rates, and we also sell single items to walk-in customers. Same stock and same testing either way — tell us which you are and we will quote accordingly.

faqs.question: Can I return or exchange something that does not fit?
faqs.answer: Yes — we offer hassle-free returns and exchanges. If a part turns out to be wrong for your machine, bring it back with the invoice. We would far rather exchange it than have you stuck with something unusable.

faqs.question: Do you stock old or obsolete parts?
faqs.answer: Often, yes — it is one of the things we are known for. We still carry DDR2 and DDR3 memory, i3 2nd-generation processors and PCI serial and parallel cards. If a working machine needs one discontinued part, ask before assuming it has to be replaced.

faqs.question: Will an upgrade actually help my machine, or should I replace it?
faqs.answer: Bring it in and we will tell you honestly. On an older machine still booting from a mechanical hard disk, moving to an SSD usually transforms it for a fraction of replacement cost. Where the platform genuinely is too old to be worth investing in, we will say that instead of selling you parts.

faqs.question: Which processor fits my motherboard?
faqs.answer: It depends on the socket and sometimes the BIOS revision, not just the generation number. Bring the machine or the board model number and we will confirm exactly what fits before you buy — a generation match alone is not enough.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an F processor and a plain one?
faqs.answer: An F variant has no integrated graphics, so it needs a separate display card to produce any picture at all. A plain variant has graphics built in. For an office machine the plain variant is almost always right; pick F only if you are fitting a graphics card anyway.

faqs.question: Do you assemble complete systems?
faqs.answer: Yes. Tell us the budget and what the machine is for and we will specify it from stock, assemble it, cable it properly and test it before handover. Buy the full parts list from us and assembly is included.

faqs.question: Do you repair laptops as well as sell parts?
faqs.answer: Yes — screens, keyboards, hinges, DC jacks, batteries and board-level work. We stock the PCB and flex cables and OEM components many shops will not, so a board can often be repaired rather than replaced entirely.

faqs.question: My UPS beeps and cuts out immediately. Do I need a new one?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly not. That is the classic symptom of a worn battery — a consumable that typically needs replacing every few years at a small fraction of the cost of the UPS. Bring the unit in and we will test it and fit a replacement.

faqs.question: Do you install CCTV, or only supply it?
faqs.answer: Both. We survey the site first, because camera placement matters far more than camera count, then supply, install and cable the system, size the recording drive to the retention period you need, and set up mobile viewing before we leave. We handle troubleshooting afterwards too.

faqs.question: Can you handle a whole office refresh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Bulk memory and storage upgrades, standard peripherals, network switches, CAT6 cabling and CCTV can all be quoted together. Ask about quantity rates and we will schedule the work around your business hours.

faqs.question: Where are you and when are you open?
faqs.answer: No. 117, Heber Main Road, Beema Nagar, Tiruchirappalli 620001. Open 8:00 AM to 9:00 PM. Call +91 97914 30774 or message us on WhatsApp before travelling if you need a specific part held.
